tn.quote: Yakut is a quantity language where all vowels, and many consonants, have phonemically short and long variants (e.g. see minimal pairs like /ɑt/ ‘horse’ vs. /ɑːt/ ‘name’ or /kɯrɯs/ ‘topsoil’ vs. /kɯrɯːs/ ‘curse’). Yakut also has regular word-final stress [1]. ... In particular, these studies highlight the important role of pitch cues in the vowel quantity distinction, even in languages that do not have lexical tone. ... In this sense, Yakut behaves like Finnish, with f0 distinctions between quantities appearing only on syllables that have tonal targets.
tn.cite: Vasilyeva, Lena, Anja Arnhold & Juhani Järvikivi. 2015. Duration and pitch in the vowel quantity distinction of Yakut: Evidence from spontaneous speech. In The Scottish Consortium for ICPhS 2015 (ed.), Proceedings of the 18th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS 2015, Glasgow), paper 0498, 5 pp. London: International Phonetic Association.

tn.note: Phonetic study treating Yakut as a non-tonal quantity language with regular word-final stress; f0 (measured) is a secondary cue to vowel quantity, not lexical tone. morph.stmt: Yamdena is predominantly prefixing on the verb (obligatory subject/aspect prefixes, causative f(a)-, adjectiviser/intransitiviser m(a)-, ng(a)-, k(a)-, detransitivisers tar-/tam-/tak-, nominalisers mang-, an-; Visser 2024: 'Subjects are obligatorily indexed on the verb by means of a prefix' and 'Drabbe (1926b: 54-59) lists eleven possible verbal derivational prefixes'), while nominal inflection is suffixal (plural -Ar, inalienable possessive suffixes); negation, mood, interrogation and case relations are free particles/prepositions.

morph.rootq: §2.4 pp.36-37: 'Stress assignment in Yine is not quantity (or quality) sensitive, and it is never contrastive. The most consistent aspect of stress in Yine is in the placement of primary stress, which always falls on the penultimate syllable (setting aside the exclamative construction described in §2.5.3 below). Secondary prominences frequently occur on the first syllable and on alternating syllables from left to right, excepting the syllable adjacent to the primary stress.' It is polysynthetic, agglutinating, head-marking, and almost entirely suffixing with only a handful of prefixes.' 413.prule: Stress falls on the first syllable of every noncompound word. In compounds and phrases placement depends on their structure: X-Y compounds and most noun + adjective/demonstrative constructions stress the second element, X+Y compounds the first (Alpher 1991: 8-9).
413.srule: Only in compounds and reduplications: in X+Y ('word-stress') compounds and in reduplications the first element carries primary stress and the second element secondary stress (a suffix in Y position is unstressed); X-Y compounds and noun+modifier phrases have primary stress on Y with lesser prominence on earlier members. No secondary or rhythmic stress is described within noncompound words (Alpher 1991: 8-9, 69).
413.quote: Stress is predictably on the first syllable of all noncompound forms, but is variable according to the structure of compounds and phrases. The symbols “-”, “+”, and “=” are used diacritically to indicate stress: In a sequence written with a hyphen, X-Y, X is unstressed and Y has primary stress. 416.heavy: Three-way scale for stress: H+ = long vowel (open or closed) 'the heaviest syllable type', always stressed; H = short vowel in closed syllable (coda /h/ and /'/ count as moras when not prevocalic), may be stressed but yields to adjacent CVV and is often unstressed word-finally; L = short open syllable, stressed only when the word lacks long vowels and nonfinal closed syllables. V'V(C) with identical short vowels acts as one heavy syllable.
416.dflt: light syllables carry main stress in an alternating trochaic pattern (initial in trisyllables like hé.yo.mus and in CVCV adverbs)
416.prule: Nominal stress (Blevins 2003, 'preliminary description'): every long-vowel syllable is stressed (level stress on H+H+); [HH] (two closed short-vowel syllables) doubly/evenly stressed; [LH] final stress with reduced initial; [H+H] initial stress, final CVC unstressed; [L H+]/[H H+] stress on the long vowel (preceding CVC gets secondary); in words with no long vowel and no nonfinal closed syllable, light syllables take main stress in an alternating trochaic pattern from the left (hé.yo.mus; CVCV adverbs initial). Regular exceptions: reduplicated nouns stress the first copy; V'VC sequences stress the first vowel. A handful of [LH] nouns have lexically marked initial stress. Verb stress is conditioned by inflectional class (fn. 16). Robins 1958:10 by contrast gives no placement rule: prominence is 'features of tempo and style' and 'the same word may have any one of its syllables prominent according to the style, tempo, and rhythmic pattern of the sentence.'
416.srule: Blevins 2003 (nouns; impressionistic, 'preliminary'): three degrees of word stress, but primary vs secondary transcribed only where clearly distinguishable. Non-primary stresses are weight-driven: every long-vowel syllable is stressed (even stress in [H+ H+]); both syllables of [HH] disyllables carry equal stress; a closed syllable before a long-vowel syllable has secondary stress ('è'.góo); a CVC after a long vowel is stressed or unstressed (cíi.sép vs náa.wec; secondary in me.cáa.nèp); light syllables in longer words alternate trochaically (cì.no.mé.wes, tó.lo.wèhl); reduplicated nouns: primary on the first copy, secondary on the second (káh.kàh).

evidence_works.detail: Khumalo separates a lexical feature [+stress], which 'resides in certain morphemes, e.g. a. Root-initial syllables of ideophones... b. Monosyllabic first position demonstratives: lo "this one", nje "like this", la "here"' (p. 132, notes to ch. 3), from phrase-final penultimate length, which he derives by a post-lexical intonational rule: '(9) Prepausal Lengthening... Condition: All syllables are [-stress]. In this intonational rule, a vowel is epenthesized to the penultimate phrase-final syllable... The [-stress] condition is required because Prepausal Lengthening does not apply to a word incorporating a stressed syllable (see Khumalo 1981: 89-91)' (p. 196), with the examples 'Bafuna uba?' NOT *u:ba and 'Lathi gilikidi' NOT *giliki:di (p. 196). The ordinary penultimate is handled as 'penultimate syllable prominence (PSP) which is marked with the feature [+prominence], is a lexical feature of stems' and '[+prominence] deletes in the presence of [+stress] or of a final bimoric syllable' (pp. 205-206, quoting Khumalo 1981: 59); Phrase Medial Lowering carries a [-stress] condition 'because on a stressed final syllable the high tone does not delink' (p. 207). The argument is from rule interaction (lengthening and tone-delinking rules blocked by stressed syllables), not from measurement. It agrees with the entry's positions (penultimate at the stem/word level, phrase-final length, ideophone root-initial and monosyllabic-demonstrative exceptions) but labels the ordinary penultimate 'prominence' rather than 'stress', reserving [+stress] for the exception classes.

No symbols will be used to indicate stress phonemes. The word space will identify the syllable following space as the locus of the strong stress: hom ʔanšema ask me for it, but hom ʔan šema order it for me.' (ʔan-šema carries the indirective PREFIX ʔan-, so stress falls on a prefix when one is present; the rule refers to the word, not the root.) Also §15.3 p.73: incorporated substantive and verb 'are treated phonologically as separate word units, for each receives the word stress on its first syllable', and…
morph.elicq: No statement of how word stress was determined. Data basis (Preface p.11): 'This grammar, consequently, is based upon work done in a large number of brief sessions with Zuni college students, supplemented by short field trips to Zuni pueblo for intensive work with older informants.' Material types (§15.3 p.73): 'the types of material which I have collected (casual speech, stories, prayers)'. The stress section itself draws on connected speech for PHRASE stress (§1.5 p.15): 'phrasal stress fluctuates considerably with style of speech: in the more deliberate types of utterance, such as prayers, even the most commonly juxtaposed particles are each given a separate strong stress.'
morph.stmt: Overwhelmingly suffixing: 'Suffixation accounts for most of the formal machinery of word-building in Zuni. Inflections for all the word classes are formed solely by suffixes' (§8.2 p.31); 'All prefixes are derivational. Involving only some half-dozen morphemes, prefixation covers a relatively small area of the morphology as compared to suffixation' (§8.4 p.32) - the prefixes being voice (reflexive, reciprocal, indirective), subject/object plural number, inchoative, indeterminate and 'terrestrial', in five prefix positions versus six derivational suffix positions plus a final inflectional suffix slot (§9.3 p.42).

423.dq: In general, there is a main lexical stress in Chol which commonly falls on the last syllable of the word
423.prule: In general the main (lexical) stress commonly falls on the last syllable of the word (ja’ál, pixól, tyumúty, ixím); borrowed words of more than two syllables seem to follow the same pattern (alaxáx, kayetáj, kixtyañúj); compounds keep the main stress on the last syllable (tyatymúty, matye’chityám); when suffixes or enclitics are added the main stress moves to the last syllable (buch-úl, buch-ul=kú, buch-ul=tyo=kú, buch-ul-oñ=tyo=ku=lá); in yes/no questions the main stress moves to the first syllable (búch-ul).

427.dq: The prosodic domain of stress asignment is the phonological word. Primary stress (marked by preceding ˈ in the examples) is assigned to the initial syllable of a word.
427.prule: Primary stress falls on the initial syllable of the phonological word (quantity-insensitive; vowel duration is not a stress correlate and the epenthetic schwa can bear stress).
427.srule: Only in words of 4+ syllables: four-syllable words are ditrochees ˈσσˌσσ (secondary on the 3rd syllable); in 5+-syllable (polymorphemic) words placement varies — most five-syllable words 3rd syllable (some 4th), most six- and seven-syllable words 4th syllable, with exceptions; secondary stress is weak and its nature 'remains to be investigated in more detail'.

evidence_works.detail: The OPD's whole stress section is one sentence: 'In polysyllabic words the main stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable, sometimes on the ultimate or antepenultimate syllable.' (p. 6). It is written for 'Wára' as Sarsa defines it, a cluster-level unit: 'The Wára language (as defined by the present writer) comprises Wurm's Upper Peremka (Rouku) Language and, in part, Tonda Language' with 'Major Villages: Yékwa, Tékwa, Réku, Wámnefér, Ufaruwa' (p. 1), so its coverage overlaps the Rouku village that the record's source (Döhler 2018) describes as Komnzo-speaking, while its orthography was 'approved by the Wara Language Committee, a group of distinguished men representing different villages in the language area' (p. 11). Against the record: Döhler 2018 §2.4.5 (p. 71) codes primary stress on the initial syllable with left-to-right trochee/dactyl/ditrochee templates (10 100 1010); the OPD's usual penultimate placement agrees for disyllables (10) and differs from three syllables up (100 vs 010). Points of agreement with the record: 'No lexical tone contrasts have been observed in Wára.' (p. 6; record tone_cls no-tone); 'There is no phonemic length in Wára.' (p. 6); and the epenthetic vowel of an initial CC cluster is unstressed in the OPD's [kʌˈmɑm] 'don't!' and [rɜˈmɑ] 'why?' (p. 8), matching Döhler's srak [ˈsɾak] ~ [sə̆ˈɾak] 'boy' where 'stress does not shift to the initial epenthetic vowel but remains with the specified vowel' (p. 71). The OPD also reports that /e/, /æ/, /o/ 'when occuring in the stressed syllables of heavily stressed or carefully pronounced words' are pronounced as glides [ie:], [eæ:], [uo:] (p. 9), e.g. [sie:ntor] 'bring it here!', which is a stress correlate Döhler does not mention.

In a longer word secondary stress tends to fall on the first syllable of a disyllabic bound morpheme, if any (for example [íkalamùndu] 'grass-ABL'), or otherwise on odd-numbered non-final syllables (e.g. [wánatʸùŋkaṛi] 'moon'). For purposes of stress the first vowel of suffixes of the form -VC(C)V normally counts as part of the preceding morpheme. Thus [ímbamìriŋgi] not [ímbamirìŋgi]…

morph.stmt: As far as the accessible chapter shows, exclusively suffixing: every bound morpheme Breen cites follows the stem (E/I/L -ṯV, ablative -muntu/-mundu, proprietive -puna, past -nu, topicaliser -ṇV), no prefix is mentioned anywhere, and his general statements presuppose suffixes only — "Ngawun roots all begin in a single consonant" (p.25), "All bound morphemes end in a vowel or /r/" (p.28), "For purposes of stress the first vowel of suffixes of the form -VC(C)V normally counts as part of the preceding morpheme" (p.25).…
